newsitem.title: JAPAN: BP, Exxon to ride wave of Japan oil market reform.
newsitem.headline: BP, Exxon to ride wave of Japan oil market reform.

text.p: Two of the world's biggest oil companies are betting that reforms in Japan, which have all but devastated earnings for domestic firms, will allow them not only to survive, but to thrive in the country's war-torn retail gasoline market, analysts said.

"The timing is good for these companies, and they are experienced at surviving," said the director of research and development at a major Japanese oil firm, who asked not to be named. "They have been doing it all over the world for the past 100 years."

With Japan oil companies shuttering gasoline service stations with abandon and profit margins at the pump withering, the allure of Japan's newly liberalised oil products market depends on the eye of the beholder.

"While liberalisation of Japan's refining and marketing sector has essentially been bad news for domestic companies...the changes are being received as good news by foreign firms," said Kang Wu, an oil industry analyst with the East-West Center in Hawaii.

This week, British Petroleum Co Plc said it had agreed with supermarket chain Iseya Kosan to build and operate up to 100 filling station-cum-supermarkets, the first foreign firm in post-war Japan to enter the retail gasoline business.

BP's new stations, the first of which is to open by the end of this year, will also take advantage of new legislation expected in 1998 allowing self-service pumps, as well as potential reforms allowing retailers to diversify their supply sources.

Also this week, two of U.S. oil major Exxon's Esso subsidiaries, which already held a 49 percent holding in Japan refiner and retailer General Sekiyu KK, dug in even deeper by upping their joint holding in the firm to 50.1 percent, giving Exxon the reins to the company.

Wu said a wave of Japanese market reforms since 1995 has effectively flushed Japan's refiners and marketers from the protective umbrella of government price fixing and opened the import and export of oil products to one and all.
The measures, which left refiners to bear the losses from affiliated retailers on their own, made it all too clear that, of Japan's 59,000 service stations, more than a third are unnecessary.
The industry has been struggling to survive on razor-thin profit margins since deregulation busted their oil product import monopoly.
The newly competitive environment has already sparked a wave of cooperative pacts in the industry, as companies strive to cut costs in the face of falling gasoline margins.

In June, Japanese refiner Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd and Mobil Sekiyu KK, a subsidiary of Mobil of the U.S., announced a sharing arrangement in their oil distribution that will save them a combined 1.2 billion yen ($10.1 million) annually.

"These are exactly the conditions which can be used to the advantage of foreign firms with the size and standing to both weather the competitive environment and, at the same time, take advantage of falling wholesale prices," Wu added.
On Friday, a BP official in Tokyo said a push by Japan over the last year to speed deregulation played a pivotal role in the timing of the new deal.
"Government approval for this deal would have been a lot more difficult a year ago than it is today," the official said.
